title: Properties of Geometrical Figures — A: Similarity

findings.finding: Vary vertex order while preserving the correspondence between the existing triangles.
findings.breakdown: This makes corresponding order visible beyond one fixed spelling of a similarity statement.
findings.checked: The diagram gives D ↔ L, E ↔ K and F ↔ J. All proposed completions follow these correspondences.

repair.proposal: Append under Question 1's existing instruction: “Predict each matching order before completing.” Using the diagrams in 1c: (i) DEF ∼ ___; (ii) EFD ∼ ___; (iii) FDE ∼ ___; (iv) DFE ∼ ___. Answers: LKJ, KJL, JLK, LJK. Follow with ___ ∼ KLJ. Answer: EDF. The triangle pair stays fixed; only the vertex order varies.

findings.doneWhen: The short sequence and unpatterned follow-up appear after 1c.

findings.finding: The rectangle demonstration does not supply the grid-construction method needed for the first sloping-sided figures.
findings.breakdown: Students can multiply the parallelogram's horizontal side and height correctly while retaining its original one-square horizontal displacement. The resulting figure has different angles. Multiplying side lengths and stating that angles must remain equal do not show how to position the new vertices.
findings.checked: The preceding teaching explains correspondence, equal angles and multiplying lengths. Neither p12-scale-factor-figures nor the rectangle example demonstrates scaling horizontal and vertical displacements along a sloping edge.
findings.assumptions: Elementary grid counting is prior knowledge; constructing enlargements by scaling vertex displacements is not established. Calculator use does not affect this issue.

repair.proposal: Before p13-q1-a, show a miniature grid example: “This edge moves 1 square right and 3 squares up. At scale factor 2, multiply both moves by 2: move 2 squares right and 6 squares up.” Draw the original and enlarged edge, then state that the same method positions the other vertices.

findings.doneWhen: A sloping-edge construction explicitly scales both grid displacements before students construct the parallelogram.

findings.finding: Extend the photograph question to reversing and combining changes of scale.
findings.breakdown: The existing dimensions support a concrete comparison between successive enlargements and one overall enlargement.
findings.checked: 172/129 = 120/90 = 4/3; the reverse factor is 3/4. Multiplying 172 and 120 by 1.5 gives 258 and 180, twice the original dimensions. Finding factors and scaling lengths are available by this topic's end.
findings.assumptions: These are optional further parts of the existing photograph question.

repair.proposal: Append to p20-q6: (a) The enlarged photograph is reduced back to 129 mm by 90 mm. What scale factor is used? Answer: 3/4. (b) The 172 mm by 120 mm photograph is enlarged again by a factor of 1.5. What are its new dimensions? Answer: 258 mm by 180 mm. (c) What single scale factor takes the original photograph to this final photograph? Answer: 2.

findings.doneWhen: The optional parts retain the photograph context and ask one question per part.

findings.finding: The first nested-triangle task simultaneously removes correspondence markers, requires recognition of similarity from parallel lines, and requires assembling a whole corresponding side.
findings.breakdown: Students must identify the top and whole triangles and compare 9 cm with 12 cm, rather than treating the adjacent 3 cm segment as the corresponding side.
findings.checked: p31 supplies ordinary corresponding-side problems. p32 progressively changes orientation and introduces shared vertices, but retains explicit correspondence markers and complete side lengths. Neither supplies the combination first required in p33-q3-a. The later scaffold in p37 occurs after this task.
findings.assumptions: Corresponding angles on parallel lines are prior knowledge from angle work. The difficulty is coordinating the representation and side selection.

repair.proposal: Add to p33-q3-a: “The parallel lines give equal corresponding angles, so the top triangle is similar to the whole triangle. Sketch these two triangles separately and label the whole left side 9 + 3 = 12 cm before forming your proportion.”

findings.doneWhen: The first nested task bridges triangle identification and whole-side assembly while leaving students to form and solve the proportion.

findings.finding: The shared-side trapezia require a proportion that cannot follow the instruction to always place the unknown in the numerator.
findings.breakdown: The stated correspondence gives x/7 = 63/x, or its reciprocal. Either choice puts x in a denominator. The preceding models do not explain this exception or the resulting squared unknown, leaving students without a route consistent with the advertised method.
findings.checked: BC ↔ EF and EF ↔ AD give x/7 = 63/x. For a positive length, multiplying by 7x gives x² = 441 and x = 21 cm. Earlier teaching and practice do not model a shared length occupying both correspondence roles.
findings.assumptions: Basic equation solving and square roots may be prior knowledge from the separate algebra booklets. The finding concerns the conflicting instruction and this new similarity setup, not unsupported arithmetic.

repair.proposal: Change the p30 instruction to “Where possible, put the unknown in the numerator to make the equation easier to solve.” Beside Q5, add: “BC ↔ EF and EF ↔ AD, so x/7 = 63/x. The shared length occurs in both ratios, so it cannot appear only in numerators. Multiplying both sides by 7x gives x² = 7 × 63 = 441. A length is positive, so x = 21 cm.”

findings.doneWhen: The instruction allows the necessary exception, and the shared-side proportion is explicitly connected to its positive solution.

findings.finding: Use the existing rectangles to compare their length and area multipliers.
findings.breakdown: The numerical comparison exposes the effect of scaling both dimensions without requiring a general area-scaling rule.
findings.checked: A has area 4 × 2.5 = 10 cm². B has width 3.75 cm and area 22.5 cm². The length multiplier is 1.5 and the area multiplier is 2.25. Similarity and rectangle area suffice.
findings.assumptions: Rectangle area is prior knowledge, as required by the existing task.

repair.proposal: After Question 6b, append optional parts referring to 6a: (i) Find the area of rectangle A. Answer: 10 cm². (ii) What number multiplies A's length to give B's length? Answer: 1.5. (iii) What number multiplies A's area to give B's area? Answer: 2.25. (iv) Explain why these multipliers differ. Answer: Both dimensions are multiplied by 1.5, so area is multiplied by 1.5 × 1.5 = 2.25.

findings.doneWhen: The optional numerical follow-up compares the two multipliers using the existing rectangles.

findings.finding: The Chris practice question repeats the complete worked example without an explicit retrieval or comparison purpose.
findings.breakdown: The stem, shadow lengths, reference height and mathematical diagram givens are unchanged, so the later task can be answered by copying the demonstrated result.
findings.checked: Both tasks give Chris' shadow as 1.2 m and a 1 m stick's shadow as 0.8 m, with the same triangle arrangement and correspondence cues. No instructional purpose for repeating the task is stated.
findings.assumptions: The later exercise provides independent application of the demonstrated method.

repair.proposal: Replace p36-q1b with: “Chris' shadow is 2.4 m long and a 1 m vertical stick has a shadow that is 1.5 m long. Determine Chris' height.” Change both shadow labels in its diagram accordingly. Answer: 1.6 m.

findings.doneWhen: The later copy retains its structure with fresh values and consistent diagram labels and answer.

findings.finding: Extend the existing map question by doubling every printed length.
findings.breakdown: Students connect an enlarged map with a smaller scale denominator while checking that actual distances remain unchanged.
findings.checked: The original scale is 1:300000. Doubling image lengths gives 1:150000; 9.2 cm becomes 18.4 cm, representing 27.6 km. All required methods are available by this topic's end.
findings.assumptions: Every printed map length is doubled uniformly.

repair.proposal: Append to p53-q5: (c) The map is enlarged so that every printed length doubles. What is its new scale? Answer: 1:150000. (d) How far apart on the enlarged map are the towns that were 9.2 cm apart? Answer: 18.4 cm. (e) Use the enlarged map's scale to calculate the actual distance between these towns. Answer: 27.6 km.

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up retains the original map context and has one question per part.

findings.finding: Compare reduction, congruence and enlargement while keeping the original rectangle fixed.
findings.breakdown: Only the multiplier changes, making the relationship between scale factor and image size visible.
findings.checked: The existing exercise changes figures as well as scale factors. All proposed dimensions follow by multiplying the original dimensions, and half-square dimensions already occur in the guided practice.
findings.assumptions: The further parts use the existing instruction to enlarge or reduce the diagram.

repair.proposal: After p14-h, add further parts using the same rectangle, 4 squares wide and 2 squares high. Add only this instruction: “Predict whether each image will be smaller, congruent or larger before drawing.” (i) Scale factor 0.5. Answer: 2 by 1 squares, smaller. (j) Scale factor 1. Answer: 4 by 2 squares, congruent. (k) Scale factor 1.5. Answer: 6 by 3 squares, larger. (l) Scale factor 2. Answer: 8 by 4 squares, larger. Follow with an unpatterned part (m), scale factor 0.75. Answer: 3 by 1.5 squares, smaller. The original shape stays fixed throughout.

findings.doneWhen: The run varies only the multiplier and ends with the unpatterned question.

findings.finding: The parallel-line triangle questions precede the teaching that equal corresponding angles are sufficient for triangle similarity.
findings.breakdown: Students must replace parallel arrows with equal-angle relationships and then infer similarity. Earlier polygon teaching requires equal angles together with proportional sides; it does not establish the triangle criterion needed to justify finding those side ratios.
findings.checked: Earlier nested questions supply correspondence symbols. The first explicit statement that equal corresponding angles prove triangle similarity occurs in p29-q9-root, which also provides a suitable parallel-line application.
findings.assumptions: Parallel-line angle relationships are prior knowledge from the separate Angle Relationships material. The triangle similarity criterion is not established before these questions.

repair.proposal: Move p29-q9-block, including its introductory criterion and both parts, immediately before p27-g.

findings.doneWhen: The equal-angle criterion and its parallel-line application precede p27-g and p27-h.

findings.finding: The shortcut claims to cover both ratio orientations but supplies operations for only 1:n.
findings.breakdown: Applying the displayed multiplication to find an original length at scale 100:1 gives 300 cm instead of 0.03 cm for Q4-f-i. The corresponding division error affects finding image lengths in Q5-f.
findings.checked: The diagram explicitly displays 1:n, so its operations are correct for that form. However, the accompanying announcement also includes n:1 without supplying its reversed operations. Earlier ratio-table teaching provides a valid alternative but does not resolve the newly advertised shortcut's coverage.
findings.assumptions: Students may use the shortcut for either form named in its introduction. Calculator use is irrelevant.

repair.proposal: Beside the diagram add: “For image:original = n:1, reverse the operations: original length = image length ÷ n; image length = original length × n.”

findings.doneWhen: Both advertised ratio orientations have their operations explicitly stated.

findings.finding: Keep the image length fixed while changing the scale's magnitude and orientation.
findings.breakdown: The sequence isolates how reversing the ratio changes whether the original is larger or smaller than the image.
findings.checked: The proposed original lengths are 48, 24, 6 and 3 cm, followed by 7 mm. These follow from the existing image:original convention and require only the topic's methods. No equivalent fixed-image run appears in the supplied practice.
findings.assumptions: The shortcut's treatment of n:1 is clarified as proposed in the retained finding.

repair.proposal: After s5-p32-q4-f, add further parts under the existing instruction. Add only: “Predict whether each actual length will be greater or less than 12 cm before calculating.” (g) Scale 1:4, scaled distance 12 cm. Answer: 48 cm. (h) Scale 1:2, scaled distance 12 cm. Answer: 24 cm. (i) Scale 2:1, scaled distance 12 cm. Answer: 6 cm. (j) Scale 4:1, scaled distance 12 cm. Answer: 3 cm. Follow with an unpatterned part (k): scale 5:1, scaled distance 35 mm. Answer: 7 mm. Only the scale changes within the four-part run.

findings.doneWhen: The four-part run holds the image length fixed, uses one prediction instruction and ends with the unpatterned question.

protectedGroups.observation: Matching angle marks determine correspondence despite changes in orientation.
protectedGroups.varies: The orientation of the triangles and the symbols used for matching angles.
protectedGroups.invariant: Two separate triangles, two marked angle correspondences and the same side-angle-statement response structure.

protectedGroups.observation: Separating a combined diagram makes the same correspondence procedure available.
protectedGroups.varies: Intersecting triangles become nested triangles.
protectedGroups.invariant: A shared vertex, parallel sides, the redraw hint and the correspondence task.

protectedGroups.observation: Equal rectangle angles do not establish similarity; corresponding dimensions must change by the same factor, which need not be an integer.
protectedGroups.varies: Whether width and height ratios agree, including equal heights and a non-integer enlargement.
protectedGroups.invariant: Both figures are rectangles with equal corresponding angles.

protectedGroups.observation: Equal corresponding angles can accompany either proportional or non-proportional side lengths.
protectedGroups.varies: Whether all corresponding-side ratios agree.
protectedGroups.invariant: Each pair consists of pentagons with equal corresponding angles.

protectedGroups.observation: Rotation preserves similarity.
protectedGroups.varies: The orientation of the larger rectangle.
protectedGroups.invariant: The larger rectangle's dimensions and its ratio to rectangle A.

protectedGroups.observation: Halving the enlargement factor halves each corresponding image length.
protectedGroups.varies: The scale factor changes from 5 to 2.5.
protectedGroups.invariant: The original triangle, its side lengths, its orientation relative to the image, and the required image sides.

protectedGroups.observation: Reversing original and image changes an enlargement factor into its reciprocal reduction factor.
protectedGroups.varies: Direction of the mapping.
protectedGroups.invariant: The same two triangles and their dimensions.

protectedGroups.observation: Reciprocal factors also occur for a non-integer enlargement.
protectedGroups.varies: Direction of the mapping.
protectedGroups.invariant: Triangles R and Q with the same dimensions.

protectedGroups.observation: Separate redraws demonstrate complete corresponding lengths before students construct those lengths independently.
protectedGroups.varies: Availability of supplied redraws and whole-side labels.
protectedGroups.invariant: Nested similar figures whose larger side includes the smaller side and an extension.

protectedGroups.observation: The same original sloping length produces different image lengths when the base ratio changes.
protectedGroups.varies: Original base: 1 cm then 2 cm.
protectedGroups.invariant: Original sloping side 3 cm, image base 3 cm, orientation and unknown image sloping side.

protectedGroups.observation: A known sloping-side pair supports finding either an image base or an original base.
protectedGroups.varies: Which base is known and which is unknown.
protectedGroups.invariant: Corresponding sloping lengths 4 cm and 15 cm, triangle orientation and correspondence.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing the measurement unit and numerical scale preserves the scaling procedure.
protectedGroups.varies: The sloping lengths and known base are ten times as large numerically and use millimetres.
protectedGroups.invariant: Scale factor 15/4, correspondence and unknown smaller base.

protectedGroups.observation: A split boundary must be assembled into the whole corresponding side before calculating a factor.
protectedGroups.varies: Orientation, polygon type and numerical lengths.
protectedGroups.invariant: Nested similar figures with a corresponding whole side given as two segments.

protectedGroups.observation: With the reference fixed, changing the target shadow changes the height proportionally.
protectedGroups.varies: The giraffe's shadow length.
protectedGroups.invariant: Reference height 0.5 m, reference shadow 2 m and the height-to-shadow relationship.

protectedGroups.observation: The large triangle uses the complete distance from the observation point, including both adjacent intervals.
protectedGroups.varies: Context, numerical lengths and, finally, measurement units.
protectedGroups.invariant: Nested triangles, a common sightline and the separate-triangle label scaffold.

protectedGroups.observation: The ratio direction must change when the unknown moves to the other figure, while corresponding sides stay paired.
protectedGroups.varies: Which figure contains the unknown and therefore which ratio direction is used.
protectedGroups.invariant: The same triangle pair and the same known corresponding bases.

protectedGroups.observation: An unknown base segment must be distinguished from the whole corresponding base.
protectedGroups.varies: Whether the unknown is a corresponding complete side or the remaining segment of that side.
protectedGroups.invariant: A smaller triangle on the right with its left side parallel to the outer left side, and a 6 cm right-hand base segment.

protectedGroups.observation: Within each pair, students must distinguish finding an original length from finding an image length at the same scale.
protectedGroups.varies: The known quantity and requested direction, with corresponding changes in units.
protectedGroups.invariant: The scale and practical representation within each pair.

protectedGroups.observation: A ratio scale applies equally to millimetres and centimetres when both quantities use the same unit.
protectedGroups.varies: The unit.
protectedGroups.invariant: The 1:500 scale and one map unit.

protectedGroups.observation: Doubling original length doubles image length at fixed scale; halving the scale denominator doubles image length for the same original distance.
protectedGroups.varies: Original length or scale denominator, one at a time; equivalent units also change between r03 and r04.
protectedGroups.invariant: The image length is the unknown throughout.

protectedGroups.observation: Original length changes proportionally with image length or with the scale denominator.
protectedGroups.varies: Image length or scale denominator, one at a time.
protectedGroups.invariant: The original length is the unknown throughout.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing one length changes the scale, while changing both lengths by the same factor preserves it.
protectedGroups.varies: Original length, then image length, then both lengths together with a unit change.
protectedGroups.invariant: The scale is the unknown throughout.
